setting: a cybersecurity training startup selling to schools (Northgate Secure)
prompt: I need a concise recommendation for Jane Patel, our COO, on whether we should raise the annual license fee for our school‑focused cybersecurity platform, Northgate Secure, from $4,500 to $5,500 per institution starting July 1, 2027. We currently serve 120 schools, generating $540,000 in ARR, with an average churn of 8% per year and a CAC of $1,200 per new school. Our internal model assumes a five‑year customer lifetime, giving an LTV of $30,000 (5 × $4,500 × (1‑0.08)ⁿ). We project that the price hike could lift ARR by 15% but might also push churn up to 12% and reduce new sign‑ups by 10 schools per quarter. We’re preparing a $2 M Series A round in Q4 2027 and need to show a clear path to $1.5 M in ARR by the end of 2028. I’m assuming schools will accept the increase without negotiating discounts, but I don’t know how our main competitor’s upcoming “SecureClass” pricing—rumored to be $4,800—will affect our positioning. Please give me one recommendation, outline the three biggest ways this change could fail, and tell me what metric (e.g., churn exceeding 10% in Q3 2027) would make us stop or pivot.

setting: a meal-kit company for athletes (Stride Kitchen)
prompt: I’m putting together a short brief for our COO, Maya Patel, about whether we should roll out the new “Performance Pro” kit in the Pacific Northwest this quarter. We launched the pilot on Jan 15 2024 with 3,200 active subscriptions at an average basket of $48, giving us $153,600 in monthly revenue. Our current CAC is $115, churn is 4.8 % per month, and we calculate LTV at $560 based on a 12‑month horizon. We have $250 k left in development funds and runway for 7 months at the current burn rate of $36 k/month. The plan assumes we can negotiate a 15 % discount with the protein‑powder supplier, which would lower the kit cost from $30 to $25.50 per unit, and that the new regional distributor will take a 10 % commission. The competitor “PeakFuel” sells a similar kit for $55 including shipping, which we’ve been using as a benchmark, but they bundle a free shaker that we don’t. We haven’t priced the extra $0.75 per kit for increased packaging disposal in Washington, and we still don’t know the exact regulatory classification of our protein blend in California, which could affect labeling. I need one clear recommendation for Maya, the top three ways this launch could fail, and the specific sales metric (e.g., hitting $500 k in quarterly revenue) that would make us stop or pivot.

setting: a property-management app for small landlords (Rowan Rentals)
prompt: I’m the VP of Growth at Rowan Rentals, the property‑management SaaS we built for owners of under‑10‑unit portfolios. I need a concise brief for our CEO, Maya Patel, on whether we should raise the base subscription from $15 to $18 per month starting 1 Oct 2026. As of 1 July 2026 we have 12,000 active landlords, an average churn of 5% per quarter, and we’ve just signed a pilot with 300 new users in Q2 that will convert to full payers by Q4. Our current ARR calculation (12,000 × $15 × 12 = $2.7 M) assumes churn is zero, which it isn’t, and we haven’t factored the $0.50 per‑user support cost we’ve recently added. I’m assuming churn will stay at 5% and that the price bump won’t affect acquisition cost, which is $30 per new landlord based on the last 6 months. The unknowns are the compliance filing fees we’ll incur in three new states (estimated between $8k–$12k each) and the exact impact on conversion from the $18 price (early tests suggest a 3% drop, but we lack hard data). Please give Maya one recommendation (raise, keep, or test), list the main ways this could fail, and tell me what metric (e.g., net ARR falling below $2.5 M after 6 months) would make us stop or change course.

setting: a podcast hosting and ad-insertion company (Echo Harbor)
prompt: I need a concise briefing for our CEO Maya Patel. Echo Harbor currently hosts 12,450 podcasts and generates $4.2 M in ARR, with an average subscription of $350 per pod and a churn rate of 4.8% per quarter. We’re considering launching a “Premium Ad‑Insertion” tier priced at $500 per pod per year, and we assume 20% of our existing customers will upgrade within the first six months. That would add roughly $1.2 M in ARR (12,450 × $500 × 0.20), but we haven’t factored the $15,000‑monthly increase in support staff needed for the higher‑touch service, nor the $0.02 CPM cost for additional ad impressions. We also assume the new tier won’t cannibalize our standard plan, even though historically we’ve seen a 3% migration when we add features. The unknown we can’t quantify yet is how the EU’s upcoming privacy regulation (effective 1 Oct 2026) will restrict our ability to target ads for the 22% of our advertisers based in Europe. Please give Maya one recommendation on whether to roll out the tier now, list the main ways this could fail, and specify the metric (e.g., net ARR growth under 5% after 12 months) that would make us stop or pivot.

setting: a dental-supply e-commerce business (Brightside Dental Supply)
prompt: I need a quick, data‑driven opinion for Maya Patel, our COO, on whether we should raise the price of the BrightSide Pro‑Clean Kit from $85 to $95 effective July 1, 2024. Our current unit economics are: CAC $28 (based on Q1‑Q2 2024 data), LTV $210, and gross margin 18% on the $85 price. We sell roughly 1.5 million kits per year, and the average order value is $120 with a 2% conversion rate from site visits (we assume that conversion stays flat). The marketing budget for Q3‑Q4 2024 is $3.2 million, and we plan to allocate an extra $500 k to a new Instagram campaign. The only unknown is how the upcoming FDA guidance on packaging materials, slated for release in September 2024, will affect our shipping and compliance costs—no estimates yet. Please give me one recommendation on the price change, list the main ways this could fail (e.g., margin erosion, churn increase, regulatory surprise), and tell me what specific result (e.g., a 5% drop in monthly repeat orders) would make us stop or pivot the plan. Thanks.

setting: a clinical-trial recruitment platform (Meridian Trials)
prompt: I’m the VP of Growth at Meridian Trials and need a concise briefing for our CFO, Elena Marquez, on whether we should raise the subscription price for our tier‑2 sponsor package from $115 to $140 per trial, effective 1 Nov 2024. We currently have 820 active tier‑2 sponsors (as of 31 Mar 2024) with an average churn of 4.8% per quarter and a CAC of $28 per sponsor. Our internal model assumes a 10% conversion from the free pilot to paid tier‑2 and projects a 12% increase in net new sponsors each quarter after the price change. That would push quarterly revenue from $94,300 to $114,600, giving us an extra $20,300 per quarter. However, we have not priced the mandatory third‑party data‑privacy audit that the new EU DPA amendment will require; the audit cost is an unknown but could be $15k per quarter. Also, the model mistakenly adds $2,300 to the revenue lift without subtracting the $28 CAC for the expected new sponsors. I need one recommendation on whether to implement the price increase, the three biggest ways this plan could fail (including the audit cost and the arithmetic error), and the specific metric—if quarterly churn exceeds 6% after two quarters or the audit cost exceeds $12k per quarter—that would make us stop or rethink the change.

setting: a ride-share bike maker adding a rental fleet (Cobalt Cycles)
prompt: I need a concise briefing for Maya Patel, our COO, on whether we should launch the Cobalt Cycles rental fleet in Metroville this quarter. We plan to deploy 5,000 bikes at a unit cost of $1,200 each, aiming for a break‑even in 12 months. I’m assuming 70 % of rides will come from our existing ride‑share users, and that each bike will average 2 rides per day at $3 per ride. That gives a projected monthly revenue of 5,000 × 2 × 30 × $3 = $900,000. Our CAC is $25, and we expect a churn of 8 % per month. We have budgeted $6 M for purchase, $1.2 M for staffing, and $0.8 M for marketing, but we haven’t included insurance, which a competitor (BluePedal) estimates at $0.15 per bike per day. The unknown is the city’s new congestion‑pricing fee of $0.05 per mile, which could add $10 K–$20 K per month depending on usage. Please give me one recommendation, outline the three biggest ways this rollout could fail, and tell me what metric (e.g., sustained monthly net loss over $150 K for two consecutive months) would make Maya pull the plug or adjust the plan.

setting: an e-signature tool for freelancers (Penstroke)
prompt: I’m the head of product at Penstroke, our e‑signature platform for freelancers, and I need a quick analysis for CFO Maya Patel. As of 1 Sep 2024 we have 12,500 monthly active freelancers generating an ARPU of $12 (Q2 2024 data). Monthly churn is 5% and we spend $30 to acquire each new user. We’ve been modelling LTV as $12 ÷ 0.05 = $240, assuming churn will stay flat if we raise the basic plan price from $12 to $15 starting 1 Oct 2024. The price hike would add $3 × 12,500 ≈ $45,000 of monthly revenue, which we think will extend our current runway of $1.2 M to cover a $3 M Series A round we aim to close by 31 Dec 2024. We also plan a new “Enterprise” tier at $8 per user per month, assuming 10% of our base will upgrade and that the incremental support cost is negligible. The unknown is how churn and upgrade rates will actually respond to the price change and the competitive reaction from SignFlow, which recently dropped its freelancer plan to $11. I need one recommendation on whether to proceed, the main ways this could fail, and the specific result (e.g., churn rising above 8% in the first month) that would make us stop or pivot.

setting: a farm-equipment leasing marketplace (Greenfurrow Leasing)
prompt: I need a quick, actionable brief for our CFO, Maya Patel, on whether we should roll out a 15 % discount on our standard 5‑year tractor lease package. The plan is to announce the discount on 2024‑05‑01 and run it for three months. We currently have 620 active leases averaging $20,000 per year, giving us about $12.4 M in annual recurring revenue. Our margin on each lease is 28 % after fuel‑service fees, which we estimate at $1.2 M annually. I’m assuming the average lease length will stay at four years, and that the discount will increase new sign‑ups by 12 % month‑over‑month, pushing total leases to 720 by September. The unknown is the regulatory filing timeline for the new discount structure under the state agricultural leasing act; we haven’t confirmed if a notice‑of‑change filing is required before May. Please give Maya one clear recommendation (go ahead, hold, or redesign), list the main ways this could fail (e.g., margin erosion, compliance breach, unexpected default spikes), and specify what metric or event—such as the discount driving net margin below 20 % or a regulator flagging the change—would make us stop or pivot.

setting: a museum ticketing and membership platform (Atlas Arts Pass)
prompt: I need a quick, data‑driven brief for Maya Patel, our COO, ahead of the board meeting on 15 Oct 2026. We’re considering raising the annual Atlas Arts Pass price from $99 to $119 starting 1 Jul 2025. Our current base is 12,000 members with an average monthly usage of 3 visits per member, and we estimate CAC at $30 per acquisition. I’m assuming a 5 % quarterly churn and that the price hike will lift ARPU by 15 % while keeping the conversion rate steady. The projected incremental revenue over the next 12 months is $2.3 M, which should extend our runway from $500 k to roughly $1.2 M after accounting for the $200 k marketing spend we plan for the rollout. The unknown is the additional compliance cost we’ll face to store European user data under GDPR, which our legal team hasn’t quantified yet. Please give me one clear recommendation (go ahead, hold, or scrap), list the three biggest ways this plan could fail, and tell me the specific result—e.g., churn exceeding 8 % quarterly or compliance cost > $150 k—that would make us stop or revise the price increase.

setting: a boutique fitness studio chain adding an app (Juniper Studios)
prompt: Maya Patel, our CEO, is reviewing whether we should launch the Juniper Studios mobile app next quarter. We have 12 studio locations and 8,400 active members paying $120 per month. We’ve spent $250,000 on development and expect to charge $15 per month per app user. Our internal model assumes 20 % of current members (1,680 users) will subscribe, giving $25,200 in monthly app revenue, and that the app will break even in 12 months. We have 10 months of cash runway left, and we could raise an additional $500,000 at a 10 % equity stake if needed. The big unknown is the churn rate for users who might stay on the app but drop their studio membership, plus any compliance costs for handling health data. I’m asking for a concise recommendation for Maya: should we go ahead, delay, or re‑price? Also list the main ways this could fail (adoption, churn, technical, regulatory) and tell me the specific result that would make us stop or change course (e.g., revenue below a threshold or churn above a threshold). The assumption we’re making is that every app subscriber will remain a studio member.

setting: a municipal parking-permit software vendor (Acme Civic Tech)
prompt: I need a quick decision memo for our CEO, Maya Patel, on whether we should raise the municipal parking‑permit subscription price from $15 to $18 per permit per month. We currently have contracts with 30 cities (average 2,500 permits each) that started between July 1 2023 and March 15 2024, and their next renewal deadline is Dec 31 2024. Our finance model assumes a 5 % city‑budget increase for tech services this year and a 2 % churn rate after the price hike. If the hike holds, we project annual revenue of 30 × 2,500 × $18 × 12 = $1.62 million, versus $1.35 million at the current price—though the model forgets the $50k implementation fee we incur for each city’s integration, which would add $1.5 million in costs. The unknown is whether the new state data‑privacy regulation slated for implementation on Jan 1 2025 will require us to redesign the API, potentially adding $200k per city. Please give me one clear recommendation, outline the three biggest ways this plan could fail, and tell me what metric or event (e.g., churn exceeding 4 % or a regulatory block) would make us abort or pivot.

setting: a vet clinic group testing subscription wellness plans (Pinewood Vets)
prompt: I’m the head of product at Pinewood Vets, and I need a recommendation for our upcoming subscription wellness plan pilot, which we’ll present to our CFO, Maya Patel, next week. We plan to launch on June 1, 2024 with a $35 monthly fee per pet. Our market research shows 1,200 pet owners in the pilot zip code, and we estimate a 30% adoption rate, giving us 360 subscribers. I’ve calculated the customer acquisition cost (CAC) at $500 per subscriber and assumed a monthly churn of 5%, which yields a 12‑month LTV of $756. The pilot’s fixed overhead is $12,000 per month, and each claim is projected to cost $12 on average, but the exact per‑claim cost after insurance adjustments is still unknown. I also assumed that the average pet will need 1.1 visits per month, though we haven’t factored in the $8 lab fee per visit. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to proceed, outline the main ways the model could fail, and tell me what metric (e.g., subscriber count falling below 250 after 3 months) would make us stop or re‑tool the plan.

setting: a B2B invoice-financing marketplace (Fernhill Capital Exchange)
prompt: I’m drafting a pricing memo for our CFO, Hana Patel, and need a quick decision on whether to raise the discount rate on our invoice‑financing product. Right now we charge 2.5% per month on average invoices of $150,000. In Q2 2024 we processed 120 invoices (I’ve calculated $16 million in total invoice value, though the correct figure is $18 million), generating $450 k in monthly discount revenue. Our operating cost is $250 k per month, and we’re targeting 200 invoices per month by Q3 2025, assuming the default rate stays at 3% and that the market can absorb a 0.5‑point increase to 3.0% per month. The only unknown is the regulatory cap on discount rates for this segment in our primary jurisdiction, which could be 3.2% or lower. Please give me one recommendation for the rate change, list the main ways this could fail (e.g., loss of volume, higher defaults, regulatory pushback), and specify what metric or event would make us stop or adjust the plan (e.g., a drop below 10% month‑over‑month volume growth or a regulator notice). The answer is for Hana Patel, our CFO.

setting: a coffee roaster launching wholesale to offices (Bluebird Roasters)
prompt: I’m the head of business development at Bluebird Roasters and I need a concise brief for our CEO, Maya Patel, on whether we should roll out a wholesale office coffee program next quarter. We plan to launch on 2024‑10‑15 with a $12‑per‑pound price point, offering a 12‑month contract at 15 lb per month per office. Our model assumes the average office will consume exactly 5 lb per week (≈20 lb per month) and that we can secure 100 offices in the first six months. That would generate $180,000 in revenue (100 offices × 15 lb × $12) and a gross margin of 55 % based on a $5.40 cost‑of‑goods per pound. We have $250,000 in runway left, and we expect to break even by month 8. The unknown is the churn rate of office accounts after the first year, and we have no data on the incremental logistics cost for delivering to multiple office locations—our current estimate is $0 because we think our existing distribution covers it. Please give Maya one recommendation (go forward or hold), list the main ways this plan could fail, and specify the result (e.g., churn > 20 % or logistics cost > $2 per lb) that would make us stop or pivot.

setting: a language-learning platform for corporate teams (Lumen Learning)
prompt: I need a concise decision memo for our CFO, Maya Patel, about whether to increase the corporate seat price on Lumen Learning from $199 to $229 starting July 1, 2026. We currently have 250 enterprise seats across three accounts (TechNova, GreenWave, and Apex). Our internal model assumes churn will stay at 10% annually, the average contract length is 12 months, and the new price will not affect the 30% YoY growth we’ve seen in the last two quarters (Q2 and Q3 2025). We project monthly revenue at $45,000 (which we’ve calculated as $199 × 250) giving $540,000 annually, and we think the change will lift ARR by about $720,000 after one year. The CAC is $150,000 per new account, and we have $3 million in runway. The unknown is whether our main competitor, Polyglot Corp, will announce a similar price hike in August, which could shift a 15% share of our pipeline. Please give Maya one recommendation on the price change, outline the main ways this could fail (e.g., churn spikes, pipeline loss, runway impact), and specify what metric or event would make us stop or reverse the new pricing.

setting: a solar-installer lead-generation site (Sunrow Leads)
prompt: I’m drafting a quick update for Jane Patel, our CEO, and I need a clear recommendation from you. Sunrow Leads currently spends $45,000 per month on Google Ads at a $12 cost‑per‑click, generating roughly 3,750 clicks. Our historic conversion from click to signed installer contract is 4%, giving us about 150 new contracts a month with an average contract value (ACV) of $5,000, so monthly revenue is roughly $750,000. I’m proposing a new pricing tier that would raise the ACV by 15% to $5,750 but we expect the conversion rate to dip by 1.5 percentage points to 2.5% because installers will balk at the higher price. The assumption is that the higher ACV will more than offset the loss in volume, giving us $862,500 in revenue at the new rates. We haven’t accounted for a $3,000 platform fee that the ad network added last quarter – an arithmetic slip I realized after the last board deck. The real unknown is whether a competitor, BrightSolar, will launch a bundled lead‑service on 15 Oct 2024 that could steal half of our clicks. Please give me one recommendation for Jane, outline the main ways this plan could fail (including the hidden fee and competitor move), and tell me what result (e.g., revenue dropping below $700k for two consecutive months) would make us stop or change course.

setting: a SaaS tool for wedding planners (Evermore Planner)
prompt: I’m drafting a pricing change proposal for Evermore Planner that I need to send to our CFO, Maya Patel, by 12 May 2024. Right now we have 1,200 paid wedding‑planner accounts, each paying $20 per month, giving us $24,000 MRR and $2.4 M ARR as of 31 Mar 2024. The churn has been steady at 7 % month‑over‑month and our CAC averages $45 per new user. I want to raise the subscription to $25 per month and introduce a “Premium Events” add‑on at $15, assuming a 4 % upgrade conversion from the current base within the first three months. If that conversion holds, I calculate an extra $6,000 MRR (1,200 × $5) plus $720 MRR from the add‑on (30 × $15), pushing ARR to about $3.1 M. The assumption is that the upgrade rate won’t affect churn. The unknown is how the new EU data‑residency regulation, effective 1 Jun 2024, will increase our hosting costs—our legal team hasn’t given a number yet. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to move forward with the price hike, outline the main ways this plan could fail, and tell me what result (e.g., churn rising above 10 % or ARR falling below $2.8 M after three months) would make us stop or pivot.

setting: a regional bus operator piloting on-demand shuttles (Harbor Transit)
prompt: Maya, our CFO, wants a concise briefing on whether we should go ahead with the on‑demand shuttle pilot in the Harbor District starting 1 May 2025. I’ve crunched the numbers: we expect 8,000 trips per month at a $5 fare, giving $40,000 in revenue. Variable cost per trip is $3.50, so $28,000 in variable expenses. Fixed costs are $120,000 (driver wages, depot rent, insurance) plus a licensing fee of $15,000 per month that I omitted in the initial sheet. I’m assuming 60 % vehicle utilization and that 30 % of riders will be out‑of‑town tourists who will pay a $1 surcharge. That would add $2,400 to revenue, but I haven’t factored potential fuel price spikes—fuel could rise 12 % in the next quarter, which is a real unknown. I also compared our per‑ride profit to Riverton Transit’s $2.50, but I didn’t account for their electric fleet subsidies. Please give Maya one recommendation (launch, delay, or adjust fare), list the main ways the pilot could fail, and specify what result (e.g., month‑end net contribution falling below $5,000) would make us stop or change course.

setting: an online used-textbook marketplace (Quill Exchange)
prompt: Hi AI, I’m Priya, the product lead at Quill Exchange. We have 12,000 monthly active users as of 30 Sep 2026, each posting an average of 1.8 textbook listings. Right now we charge sellers $5 per premium listing, and we’re thinking of raising it to $7 starting 15 Oct 2026. Our finance team says that with the new price the monthly revenue would be 12,000 × 1.8 × $7 = $151,200, a 15% bump over the current $131,400. Our churn is 5% per month, CAC is $22, and we calculate LTV as $9.5 ÷ 0.05 = $190 (ARPU is $9.5). We’re assuming a price‑elasticity of –0.8 for the premium tier, but we don’t actually know the true elasticity for our market segment. The change will add $5,000/month in support costs and we have a $30,000 marketing budget allocated to retain users during the transition. I need a single recommendation for our board member Maya Patel, the CFO, plus the main ways this could fail, and the result that would make us stop or pivot (e.g., net revenue growth under 5% after two quarters).
